title: One in Four Adults With a 'Normal' BMI Are Actually Obese. For South Asians, the Numbers Are Worse.
excerpt: A USC study of 5,642 Americans found that BMI misses dangerous hidden fat. For a community that develops diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights, this is a wake-up call.
body:
A major new study from the University of Southern California has found that more than one in four American adults with a 'normal' body mass index are actually obese when measured using updated diagnostic criteria — a finding with outsized implications for the South Asian diaspora, which has long been known to carry disproportionate metabolic risk at lower body weights.

The study, which analysed health data from 5,642 adults in the United States, applied a revised obesity framework proposed last year by an international panel of experts. That framework goes beyond the traditional BMI scale — which classifies anything between 18.5 and 24.9 as healthy — by incorporating waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio to build a fuller picture of dangerous visceral fat.

The Numbers Are Stark

Under the updated criteria, 25 per cent of adults previously classified as having a 'normal' BMI met the threshold for obesity. Among those already classified as 'overweight' by traditional BMI standards, more than half qualified as obese under the new framework.

"Many people assume that if their BMI says they are not obese, they don't have to worry about the many health problems linked to obesity," said Dr Brian Lee, an associate professor of clinical medicine at USC. "Our findings show that millions of Americans may already have obesity-related health impacts and may be missing needed health interventions."

The problem, Dr Lee explained, is structural. BMI measures total body weight — including muscle and bone — rather than body fat specifically. "A muscular person can have a very high BMI but not have excess fat, while someone without much muscle can have a normal BMI but have excess fat causing health problems," he said.

Why South Asians Should Be Paying Closer Attention

For the Indian diaspora, this study validates what researchers have been arguing for over two decades. South Asians carry significantly more visceral fat — the metabolically dangerous fat that accumulates around the abdomen and internal organs — at any given BMI compared to people of European descent.

The World Health Organization acknowledged this disparity back in 2004 when it recommended lowering BMI cutoffs for Asian populations: from 25 to 23 for overweight, and from 30 to 27.5 for obesity. India went further, adopting cutoffs of 23 for overweight and 25 for obesity. A landmark study from England's National Health Service found that the BMI threshold equivalent to the cardiovascular risk of a BMI of 30 in white Europeans was just 23.9 for South Asians.

The American College of Cardiology has published data showing that among South Asians in England, the BMI cutoff that predicted the same diabetes risk as a BMI of 25 in white adults was a strikingly low 19.2. At that level, most people would consider themselves perfectly healthy.

This is the phenomenon sometimes called "skinny fat" or "thin-outside-fat-inside" — and it disproportionately affects South Asians. A person of Indian origin with a BMI of 24 may have the same metabolic profile as a European-descent person with a BMI of 30.

What the Diaspora Should Do

The practical implications are clear. First, do not rely on BMI alone. If your GP tells you your weight is fine based on BMI, ask for a waist circumference measurement and a waist-to-height ratio check. For South Asian men, a waist circumference above 90 cm (35.4 inches) is a red flag. For South Asian women, the threshold is 80 cm (31.5 inches).

Second, get your metabolic markers checked — fasting glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides, and an insulin sensitivity panel — even if your BMI says you are in the healthy range. The MASALA study at Northwestern University has already demonstrated that 30 per cent of South Asian adults in the US have prediabetes by age 45, despite reporting healthier diets than other ethnic groups.

Third, prioritise exercise that targets visceral fat. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity — running, cycling, swimming, resistance training — is significantly more effective at reducing abdominal fat than gentle walking alone.

Dr Lee put it simply: "The earlier we identify people at risk, the better chance we have of improving long-term health and quality of life."

For a community where heart disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome arrive earlier and at lower body weights than the general population, this study is not an abstract finding. It is a direct call to rethink what 'healthy weight' means — and to stop trusting a number that was never designed with South Asian bodies in mind.
